title: Additional work examples
subtitle: Strategic Design Leadership Across Multiple Verticals

content.text:
Design leadership through principles

For the fashion vertical, I led design by grounding the work in clear, research-backed design principles. These weren’t abstract ideas; they were aligned to Walmart’s brand promise and distilled from customer insights. By codifying what mattered most to shoppers, the principles helped our cross-functional teams stay focused on customer value even as priorities shifted.

My role: I drove the creation and adoption of these principles, making sure they weren’t just a design artifact but a shared north star for product, engineering, and business partners. This elevated design’s voice in strategic conversations and ensured execution always tied back to customer needs.

Creating clarity for near- and long-term goals

One of the most effective ways to align teams is to paint a clear picture of the future. I facilitated design sprints and discovery projects that brought design, product, engineering, and business leaders together to imagine what our experience could look like beyond the next quarter.

My role: I guided the visioning process and mentored the staff designer who was leading the effort, ensuring we balanced imagination with feasibility. These efforts didn’t just create inspiring concepts; they gave executives and teams a tangible vision to rally around, clarifying how near-term roadmaps fit into a longer journey.

sections.title: Building a healthy pipeline of customer-driven features

content.text:
Driving discovery into a design-led backlog

For a key discovery initiative in grocery, I guided the team through a structured process: defining our design target, articulating goals and customer problems, synthesizing past research alongside new co-creation studies, creating design principles, and facilitating cross-functional ideation. We tested concepts, validated assumptions, and ultimately built a backlog driven directly by customer insights.

My role: I shaped the process end to end, making sure design played the connective role between research, ideation, and execution. The result was a backlog that reflected not just business needs, but a clear line of sight to customer value.

Conveying the direction through the customer’s eyes

As part of my design leadership, I introduced journey maps as a way to connect strategy to real human experiences. These maps illustrated the customer journey end to end, making it clear how each initiative fit into a broader story.

My role: I championed journey mapping as a leadership tool, not just a design artifact. It became a way to advocate for the customer at every step, helping executives and teams see not only what we were building, but why it mattered to people in the real world.
